title: Data Pipelines and Data Governance
learning_outcomes: Explain data Pipelines and Data Governance and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in data Pipelines and Data Governance to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study data Pipelines and Data Governance within Data Fundamentals and Preparation. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Data quality and governance shape downstream outcomes. Record where data came from, what it means, and how it was transformed before training.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: A reliable pipeline validates inputs, versions transformations, documents lineage, and defines retention and access rules. Governance makes later results explainable and reduces accidental misuse or silent changes.

items.text: Repeatable preprocessing pipelines is one of the concepts used to reason about data pipelines and data governance. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Dataset versioning
items.text: Provenance and lineage record where data came from and how it changed. Versioning allows a later result to be tied to a specific snapshot and transformation pipeline.

items.title: Monitoring changes in incoming data
items.text: Operational monitoring combines service measures such as latency, errors, and cost with task-quality measures such as relevance or failure rate. Every alert should have a threshold, owner, and response plan.

rows = [{"id": 1, "score": 8}, {"id": 2, "score": None}, {"id": 2, "score": 6}]
seen = set()
clean = []
for row in rows:
    if row["id"] in seen or row["score"] is None:
        continue
    seen.add(row["id"])
    clean.append(row)

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content.task: Try it yourself: create six synthetic records for data pipelines and data governance. Identify a quality issue, document a repeatable handling rule, and show how the rule changes the data without leaking test-set information.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
